Our group has been working on formalization of PDE theory in Lean. We began by formalizing Sobolev spaces over bounded domains, mainly following the material in Evans' PDE textbook.

Repository: https://github.com/weiran-sun/pde
The relevant files are in  PDE/SobolevSpace.

At this stage, we have constructed W^{k,p} (\Omega) as a Banach space. We will continue to formalize approximate solutions, trace operator, Sobolev embedding, Poincare inequality.

Comments, suggestions, or pointers to relevant Mathlib conventions are greatly appreciated!

Welcome! I remember our discussions (also involving @Rémy Degenne) at SLMath last October; it's nice to see you on Zulip now! There are now two distinct projects working on adding Sobolev spaces to mathlib: @Moritz Doll has formalised Sobolev spaces and the Sobolev embedding theorem in the sense of Bessel potential spaces, i.e. using Fourier multipliers. @Filippo A. E. Nuccio, @Floris van Doorn and I are formalising Sobolev spaces using the Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces (i.e., using weak derivatives). Not all of that is in mathlib yet, so some of it already is:
for example, we already have docs#ContDiffMapSupportedIn and docs#TestFunction for smooth test functions, classical distributions (including that a locally integrable function defines a distribution). The current work in progress for Bessel potential spaces lives in #33329, on Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces the place to look is #32305 (which we are updating to right mathlib right now).
Update: the current state of Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces is now in https://github.com/grunweg/SobolevSlobodeckij

About your repository, I have a question for you: what's your eventual goal for the project? Should it be a faithful formalisation of Evans' book (matching the generality there), should it demonstrate that Sobolev spaces can be formalised, be a formalisation for your group to build on, be a high-quality formalisation artefact suitable for mathlib inclusion, be a means to gather researchers interested in formalising PDE theory, or something else?

At the moment, there are quite a few places where the repository and mathlib's (intentionally very picky!) standards differ. Whether this is important at all depends on your motivation!

Hi Michael and Rémy, great to reconnect here! Thank you for your comments and questions. We have several goals for our project: first, our code is written with the goal to submit to Mathlib. In fact, we plan to submit the part we have built very soon. Evans is a good starting point. We will build the basics along Evans' way, with some possible changes in definitions or proofs as we see fit.

Second, we have other PDE formalization projects underway that make use of the Sobolev code. Eventually, we hope to build enough usable tools for the community to formalize research-level PDE analysis.

Thanks for pointing out the existing repositories. We would be happy to chat about the best way to proceed as a community, including whether there is any interest to coordinate, and if so, how.

You code looks very much LLM generated and not even close to the right generality appropriate for mathlib. So while you are free to open a PR to mathlib, the likelihood of it getting merged is pretty low.

Moritz Doll said:

You code looks very much LLM generated and not even close to the right generality appropriate for mathlib. So while you are free to open a PR to mathlib, the likelihood of it getting merged is pretty low.

Thank you very much for your feedback. This is very helpful information for us. We would like to comment on the AI and generality issues. For context, our group consists of both computer scientists and mathematicians. So in addition to formalization itself, developing tools for formalization is also among our interests.

  1. AI usage: AI is one of the tools we use to generate our code, but we don't rely on autoformalization. Our workflow involves several tools and inputs:
    -- We have developed a search engine for the Mathlib documentation to help identify relevant lemmas, theorems, definitions etc.
    -- We have developed a Lean refactoring tool to optimize our existing correct code.
    -- We design and build the basic framework of proofs and definitions by hand. The final codebase is a mixture of hand-written and AI-generated components. All the AI-generated code go through manual checking and iterations for correctness and optimization. So the overall process is carefully supervised by human.

  2. Generality: I checked Michael's Sobolev code on GitHub. Indeed, Michael's code is formulated in a more general setting than ours. Our code follows the structure in Evans' book and we have in mind the applications to PDE analysis in Euclidean spaces. We are open to make it more general.

Thanks again for your valuable feedback.

Just a note from the classical side -- I have formalised three 1D PDE results (weak solutions of conservation laws, Burgers gradient blow-up, KdV soliton) using only elementary calculus, Fubini, and ODEs over Mathlib, with zero sorry. No Sobolev, no distributions needed for these particular theorems.

They might serve as simple test cases once Sobolev spaces land -- e.g. the conservation-law weak solution API (TestFunction, weakResidual, IsWeakSolution) is deliberately stated for arbitrary flux and integrates over the open cylinder, so it should compose cleanly with whatever Sobolev / distribution infrastructure emerges.

Repo: github.com/Alektronnik/M4TH -- packages ConservationLaws, BurgersBlowUp, KdV. Happy to adapt the API once the Sobolev PRs mature.
